items.title: AI Pentest Tool AntiFox Abused To Steal AWS Credentials
items.summary: Arctic Wolf saw attackers use the AntiFox pentest platform to hit IIS servers and AWS accounts. These frameworks chain attack steps together with little human effort. In several intrusions, Alibaba Cloud systems hosting AntiFox interfaces were tied to […]
items.raw: Arctic Wolf saw attackers use the AntiFox pentest platform to hit IIS servers and AWS accounts. Arctic Wolf Labs has published research on attackers using AntiFox, an open-source, Chinese-language agentic penetration testing platform. These frameworks chain attack steps together with little human effort. In several intrusions, Alibaba Cloud systems hosting AntiFox interfaces were tied to confirmed attacks on internet-facing web services and the AWS environments behind them. Two entry points showed up. In some cases, the attackers got into a public IIS application, though Arctic Wolf couldn’t identify the vulnerability. In others, they started with a valid AWS credential obtained by means nobody knows. “Arctic Wolf is tracking the emerging use of self-hosted agentic penetration testing frameworks, including AntiFox, from public cloud infrastructure.” states the report published by Arctic Wolf, “In several recently observed intrusions, Alibaba Cloud systems hosting AntiFox interfaces were associated with confirmed malicious actions against internet-facing web services and associated AWS environments.” The IIS attacks followed a similar pattern. The IIS worker process, w3wp.exe, created an ASPX web shell and then ran commands to gather information about the system. The attackers checked the user account, listed files in the application folder, reviewed file permissions using icacls and tested whether they could write files to the website’s main folder. They then used PowerShell to read the web.config file, looking for database connection details and application settings. They also checked folders containing debug and error logs. Using credentials found in the configuration file, they tried to connect to an internal production database. Finally, they copied configuration files and logs into an upload folder that could be accessed through the website. The AWS attacks moved quickly. AntiFox used valid IAM accounts and, in some cases, an assumed EC2 role. The attackers first checked their identity and permissions within AWS. They used commands such as GetCallerIdentity, GetUser, ListUsers, ListRoles, ListPolicies and ListKeys to discover available accounts, roles, policies and access keys. They also tried to obtain an authorization token for Amazon Elastic Container Registry (ECR). items.raw: Maersk confirms a data breach involving a legacy system, while WhiteArmor claims 100GB of stolen data and demands a $5 million ransom. A.P. Moller Maersk, the Danish shipping giant, says it identified an IT security incident involving unauthorized access and data extraction from one of its local legacy systems, one inherited from a previous acquisition. “Maersk has identified an IT security incident involving unauthorised access and data extraction from one of our local legacy systems from a previous acquisition.” reads the statement published by Maersk on November 11. “Our findings so far strongly suggest no sensitive data has been disclosed. The incident is isolated to a local system, and we have found no indication that there has been any impact on other Maersk systems or customer and partner systems that connect to Maersk through integrations such as APIs and EDI.” According to Maersk, its cyber security team started a full investigation as soon as it found the problem, and it’s still going. The company says swift action secured the affected system. Its findings so far strongly suggest no sensitive data has been disclosed, and it says the incident is isolated to that one local system. Maersk has found no sign that other Maersk systems were affected, or the customer and partner systems that connect to it through integrations such as APIs and EDI. It doesn’t expect disruption for customers, who can book and manage shipments as usual. It promises updates and says it will inform any affected parties if it finds a need to. Maersk didn’t name the system, the type of data or the date of the intrusion. However, the cybercrime group WhiteArmor added the company to its Tor data leak site: WhiteArmor demanded a $5 million ransom in Bitcoin, giving Maersk 30 days to pay. The group claims to have stolen about 100 GB of data from the OCF/LF Logistics platform, which supports logistics and supply chain operations. “”Your contract-logistics arm, the former LF Logistics, runs fulfilment for many of the world’s largest consumer brands,” states the leak site . “Five million dollars is roughly four hours of that EBITDA.”” Maersk acquired LF Logistics, the company that developed the platform, from the Li & Fung Group in 2022. This could match Maersk’s reference to an old system inherited through an acquisition, although the company has not confirmed this connection. items.title: Ease of use and secure defaults in the new AWS experience
items.summary: Starting on Amazon Web Services (AWS) is now more straightforward and more secure by default than it’s ever been. Over the past several months, we rolled out a new AWS experience that changes how you start building. It brings together a set of sensible, secure defaults, and taken one at a time, it’s easy to […]
items.raw: Starting on Amazon Web Services (AWS) is now more straightforward and more secure by default than it’s ever been. Over the past several months, we rolled out a new AWS experience that changes how you start building. It brings together a set of sensible, secure defaults, and taken one at a time, it’s easy to miss the bigger picture of what we’re building and why. When we first built how you get started on AWS, cloud was a new concept. It was a world where RSS and APIs were the exciting new thing. Twenty years later, we’ve come a long way and learned a lot about how people start, build, and grow on AWS. So, before I get into the recent launches, let me state the vision plainly: Make AWS straightforward to start on without giving up the depth, the pricing, or the security that make it the right place to grow. You shouldn’t have to choose between getting started quickly and staying secure. The rest of this post builds out this idea and highlights the defaults that make it real. What developers told us For years, developers have told us a version of the same thing. They knew AWS was where they wanted to grow, but they wanted to start fast, not plan for scale on day one. The same depth that lets AWS grow with you also meant more to set up on day one. There’s a payment method to enter before you can start, a console built for experienced administrators to get oriented in, and permissions to configure before your app can run. That feedback is fair, and it’s a big part of why we keep building a better AWS. The new experience is our answer to that, and most of it comes down to sensible, secure defaults. The secure defaults behind the new experience The new AWS experience sets secure defaults for you, so your setup starts secure instead of something you harden later. The defaults are sensible ones, drawn from what we’ve learned about how people start on AWS. Here are a few and what they do: Builder ID sign-in, with two-factor protection built in. In the early days of AWS, you signed in as the account’s root user. You could set up separate identities for everyone, but that took real effort, so sharing one login was often the path of least resistance. We’ve learned a lot since then. AWS Builder ID is a personal identity that represents you as an individual, and you use it to sign in with email and password or through a social login like Google or Apple. items.title: The global socket: how threat actors are weaponizing GSocket for stealthy C2
items.summary: Threat actors are deploying GSocket on compromised Linux servers to keep encrypted remote access after the original vulnerability is patched. Learn how to detect, investigate, and remediate this activity.
items.raw: In this article When one RCE stops being just one RCE Observed attack chains How threat actors deploy and operate GSocket How GSocket reconnects without a fixed C2 address Mitigation and protection guidance References Learn More Microsoft observed multiple incidents in which threat actors deployed GSocket, an open source remote access tool, on compromised Linux servers. Threat actors used Gsocket to maintain access even after the vulnerabilities used for initial compromise were remediated. This turned a single web application compromise into persistent access that outlasted the remediation of the original vulnerabilities. Defenders investigating affected hosts should look for evidence of GSocket deployment, persistence, privilege escalation, and outbound connections, rather than treating application patching alone as complete remediation. Microsoft Defender for Endpoint telemetry shows this activity growing over recent months and concentrated on web applications and hosting environments. GSocket relays traffic through a shared public network, so there is no threat actor-owned IP address or domain to block. When one RCE stops being just one RCE Exploiting a web application vulnerability gives a threat actor command execution in the context of the web server process. That access lasts only while the vulnerability remains unpatched and the service keeps running. Patching the application or restarting the service can remove it. To keep access, threat actors typically add a persistence mechanism, and each common option has drawbacks. SSH keys added to authorized_keys are easy for administrators to find during an audit. Reverse shells depend on threat actor-controlled servers that defenders can block or sinkhole. Custom implants require ongoing development and maintenance. The same trade-offs apply when initial access comes through remote access services or cloud shell sessions. GSocket addresses these drawbacks, which helps explain why multiple unrelated threat actors have adopted it. Shared relay infrastructure. Traffic passes through the Global Socket Relay Network, a public relay service. The threat actor does not register or host any infrastructure, so there is no threat actor-owned IP address or domain to block. Organizations can still restrict access to the relay itself. items.title: Quase 70% das falhas em sistemas corporativos brasileiros são graves, diz estudo
items.summary: Falhas críticas e altas já são 68,5% das vulnerabilidades confirmadas em sistemas de empresas brasileiras, aponta estudo da BugHunt
items.raw: Quase sete em cada dez vulnerabilidades confirmadas em sistemas de empresas brasileiras entre setembro de 2025 e o mesmo período deste ano foram classificadas como críticas ou altas. O dado consta em um relatório compartilhado com exclusividade ao TecMundo pela BugHunt , plataforma nacional de recompensa por erros de segurança. A proporção saltou de 58,2% para 68,5% em comparação com os 12 meses anteriores. Segundo os pesquisadores da empresa, o avanço ocorreu principalmente por causa das falhas com gravidade alta, que cresceram de 26,3% para 40,8% do total e viraram as ocorrências mais frequentes nos testes. De modo geral, esses tipos de brecha permitem que um cliente visualize dados de outros usuários ou que um perfil comum acesse funções restritas a administradores. Na contramão, as falhas de gravidade média caíram de 36,1% para 22% e perderam espaço para as ocorrências mais severas. As falhas críticas recuaram de 31,8% para 27,8%, enquanto as de gravidade baixa subiram para 9,5%. Falhas críticas e altas já são 68,5% das vulnerabilidades confirmadas em sistemas de empresas brasileiras, aponta estudo da BugHunt Foto: Reprodução/ChatGPT Como o levantamento avaliou companhias que já mantêm programas estruturados de segurança, os números revelam os riscos remanescentes em ambientes testados de forma contínua. Conexões complexas ampliam riscos O aumento nas falhas de gravidade alta reflete a complexidade crescente dos ambientes corporativos, avaliam os pesquisadores da BugHunt . Para Caio Teles, co-fundador da empresa, os sistemas ganharam diversas camadas integrações que dependem umas das outras: Paralelamente, o estudo revelou que 15,1% dos relatórios fechados no período descreviam uma vulnerabilidade que outro pesquisador já havia enviado antes. Isto é, a mesma brecha foi encontrada por pessoas diferentes por caminhos próprios, o que indica que um atacante com intenções maliciosas também poderia descobrir o ponto fraco. Decisão de negócio correção rápida Diante desse cenário, a recomendação da BugHunt é que as organizações alterem a forma de organização dos fluxos de reparo. Em vez de seguir a ordem de chegada dos chamados, as companhias devem priorizar a gravidade das falhas confirmadas. Vanderbilt University is a private research university in Nashville, Tennessee. Founded in 1873, it now serves more than 13,800 undergraduate, graduate, and professional students across 12 schools and colleges, with programs ranging from engineering and education to law, medicine, and nursing. Its combination of teaching and research means its systems support not only everyday campus activities but also valuable academic research. According to Bleeping Computer , BYOD claims it encrypted Vanderbilt’s databases and obtained more than one million Social Security numbers, along with names, email addresses, telephone numbers, student and employee records, and research data. items.title: Part 4 – Cybersecurity journeys: What I’d tell my younger self
items.summary: Over the past few weeks, I’ve introduced you to people who fell into security from the most unexpected places, who work in domains you’ve probably never heard of, and who were honest about what the job is like after the excitement fades and the real work begins. This is the final post in a four-part […]
items.raw: Over the past few weeks, I’ve introduced you to people who fell into security from the most unexpected places, who work in domains you’ve probably never heard of, and who were honest about what the job is like after the excitement fades and the real work begins. This is the final post in a four-part series following 11 Amazon Web Services (AWS) security professionals through the real stories of how they got here and what the work actually looks like. For this last one, I wanted to end where almost every one of my conversations ended up on its own: the things people wish they’d known sooner. This one is about hard-won perspective, the kind you only get from doing the uncomfortable thing and coming out the other side. It’s about growth that doesn’t always feel like growth while it’s happening, and the advice these folks would hand to the earlier versions of themselves. If you’ve been with me since Part 1: I didn’t plan this , thank you for sticking around. I hope this last set of stories gives you something to carry into your own path. Choosing the harder room Justin Mills, Security Engineer When I asked Justin Mills where someone should start, I expected a certification or a favorite course. His answer started with two words, “seek discomfort,” and his own career shows he means it. Justin is a security engineer with more than a decade in the field, and today he consults on how AI can strengthen security detections. Detections are the rules and models that watch a system’s activity and flag the signs of an attack, and both they and AI are changing faster than most of us can keep up with. What stuck with me was how much faster everything moved after he committed to doing the hard things: he earned two promotions in roughly 2 years. So I asked him how, and his answer came back to the people around him. What surprised me was that he never went looking for them. Some came through luck, starting with the manager who hired him, and others arrived the way most good working relationships do: he got involved in projects, met the people on them, and the conversations just started flowing. He didn’t push or force any of it. “Those who are meant to be part of your career story will be part of it, no shoehorning needed.” —Justin Mills The other half of the equation was trust. items.title: Who Runs the Ransomware Group Qilin?
items.summary: The cybercrime group Qilin has emerged as the world's most active ransomware affiliate program, claiming at least 365 victim organizations in the past three months alone. But even top Russian hackers make operational security mistakes, and the administrator of Qilin has made a few key missteps over the last decade that all point to a 36-year-old man living in St. Petersburg, Russia.
items.raw: The cybercrime group Qilin has emerged as the world’s most active ransomware affiliate program, claiming at least 365 victim organizations in the past three months alone. But even top Russian hackers make operational security mistakes, and the administrator of Qilin has made a few key missteps over the last decade that all point to a 36-year-old man living in St. Petersburg, Russia. Operating since September 2022, the Russia-based ransomware group Qilin is the currently the most industrious ransomware-as-a-service gang, according to a report (PDF) this month by the cybersecurity firm NCC Group (KrebsOnSecurity profiled the administrator of the second most active ransomware group — The Gentlemen — in June). The Qilin ransomware administrator “Haise” advertising his affiliate program on the cybercrime forum RAMP. Image: Ke-la.com. Qilin attracts affiliates to hack into companies and deploy ransomware by offering them at least 80 percent of any extortion amount paid by victims. Its members practice the “double extortion” model, stealing sensitive data before encrypting systems and threatening to publish the files online. Unlike most ransomware partnerships based out of Russia, Qilin is happy to team with English-speaking affiliates, and its leader has shared on Telegram that they’ve worked with ransomware groups like Scattered Spider and RansomHub . The head of Qilin goes by the handle “ Haise ,” but they weren’t always known by this nickname. It is not uncommon for cybercriminals to change their handle periodically as an operational security (opsec) measure. Doing so is generally a smart move, because it helps to sever one’s ties to older identities that may not have been as careful on basic opsec, such as separating their real life identity from their cybercrime activities. But even those cautious criminals will sometimes have to reference their past monikers when applying for membership at a new forum. And forums eventually get hacked or seized. That is precisely what happened with Haise. The cyber intelligence platform Intel 471 records that in June 2022, Haise applied for membership to RAMP , a closely-guarded Russian cybercrime forum that was created as a haven for ransomware affiliate programs. Intel 471 has indexed direct messages from RAMP (the forum was seized by the FBI in January 2026), and those missives show the RAMP administrator approved Haise’s application, referring to this user as Haise and by their Telegram username: Alexbigboss44 . items.title: Lessons from 59 Linux Kernel Bug Reports
items.summary: Microsoft FORGE Lab researchers used codename MDASH to investigate Linux kernel vulnerabilities, resulting in 59 upstream bug reports, 33 assigned CVEs, and 38 merged fixes. The research includes eight demonstrated local root privilege-escalation exploits and examines the challenges of turning AI-generated findings into validated vulnerabilities and upstream fixes.
items.raw: In this article From scans to reports Selected findings Closing thoughts At Microsoft’s FORGE Lab , we used codename MDASH to scan a subset of Linux kernel subsystems from late May to mid-June 2026. One full-time researcher and one intern led this three-month effort, which has so far produced 59 public upstream reports and 33 assigned CVEs . We confirmed working root privilege-escalation exploits for eight of those CVEs, and fixes for 38 of our reports have been merged into mainline. Finding the bugs was only part of the work. The initial scans produced 26,502 raw findings in about two weeks, but turning those results into reproducible bugs, upstream reports, and patches took months of expert investigation and collaboration with Linux maintainers. In this post, we look back at how we went from thousands of potential findings to validated vulnerabilities and upstream fixes, and what we learned about scaling vulnerability discovery with AI. From scans to reports We focused on several core kernel subsystems, such as networking, filesystems, and security modules. Our selection criteria were straightforward: we picked security-sensitive components with no obvious dependence on specialized hardware, making QEMU-based validation simple and unified. Code scanning mainly used Sonnet 4.6 (71.1% of code-scanning tokens), GPT-5.4 (20.1%), and GPT-5.5 (7.1%). The codename MDASH scans produced 26,502 raw scan findings in about two weeks on two servers (64 cores/256 GB RAM and 32 cores/128 GB RAM), but turning that output into patches and reports took months of expert work. We filtered out low-confidence claims using codename MDASH’s confidence levels and separate fast screening agents we built, reducing the pool to 11,769 candidates. PoC-generating agents then attempted reproduction in QEMU, mainly using GPT-5.5 (77.3% of reproduction tokens), Opus 4.6 (13.2%), and GPT-5.5-cyber (9.4%). Experts then reviewed the 621 cases with PoC evidence to identify root causes, merge duplicates, and prepare upstream submissions. Figure 1 . Scan-to-report workflow. 26,502 raw findings → 11,769 screened candidates → 621 PoC-backed cases → 59 upstream reports. Where the 621 cases went Roughly one public upstream report landed from every ten PoC-backed cases: 59 reports from 621 cases (9.5%). Across those cases, the main reasons for not filing a separate new report were: 266 (42.8%) shared a root cause with another case, so one patch could fix them together. 163 (26.2%) were not reported

items.title: Google DeepMind just mathematically verified key parts of Signal
items.summary: The four-week project hints that AI could make formal verification far more practical.
items.raw: Google DeepMind researchers used agentic AI to mathematically prove, or “formally verify,” a number of the Signal protocol’s key cryptographic guarantees—a landmark development for the widely used cryptography and AI itself. Conducted as a sort of proof-of-concept project in just four weeks, the work is significant in two ways. It serves as further independent validation of the cryptography that protects massive quantities of the world's communications on platforms like the Signal app , Google Messages, and WhatsApp. And it demonstrates Google DeepMind's formal verification capabilities using a new AI framework called AlphaProof Code. More broadly, AI-aided formal verification is having a moment, but it is unclear how practical it will be for widespread use and how effective it can be at securing large amounts of code. Proponents of formal verification have long referred to it as a sort of holy grail in software security, because it uses math to check and validate that software is functioning as intended—in other words, that it doesn't have critical vulnerabilities. items.title: Remus malware claims Gmail access even after you change your password
items.summary: Developers of the infostealer Remus claim their malware can retain access to a victim’s Gmail even after a password reset.
items.raw: Changing your password should be part of recovering a compromised account. The developers of Remus Stealer are advertising a Gmail-reading feature they claim can survive that step and even session revocation. That is a serious claim. It is not, however, a demonstrated capability in the published investigation. Threat intelligence company Hudson Rock examined Remus’s promotional material and questioned both its developer and a self-described customer. Its conclusion is more cautious than the sales pitch: The material depicts a mailbox-reading interface, but it does not establish that Remus can retrieve new messages after an account has been comprehensively secured. Nor does it establish a Gmail zero-day vulnerability. What Remus is advertising According to Hudson Rock, Remus’s version 1.3.9 announcement promotes a feature that lets operators open a compromised Gmail mailbox directly from the service’s dashboard. The supplied screenshots show message lists, individual emails, and a “Mail” option attached to records of compromised devices. The announcement makes several additional claims: Operators can intercept email verification codes without collecting browser cookie files. Password changes and session revocation do not stop access. Mailbox access can be shared with other operators through links. Asked how it works, the developer described interaction with browser memory and said the malware executes and exits. The developer also claimed the service avoids Google’s anti-fraud checks, but withheld the technical details needed to assess that assertion. Remember, those are marketing statements from the seller of a criminal service, not independently verified findings. What the evidence shows Hudson Rock spoke with a person who had publicly endorsed the feature and described using it. That source said mailbox access continued after browser closure, a session reset, and a Google password change. But the correspondence does not document exactly which sessions were reset, the account settings involved, or the timing of the password change and subsequent access. The source’s independence was not established, and the statements were not accompanied by a controlled test. Hudson Rock explicitly states that its report includes neither reverse engineering of the new feature nor controlled post-recovery validation. Breaches happen every day. Don’t be the last to know. items.summary: Falso software de segurança no GitHub contamina 2 mil computadores
items.raw: Uma campanha cibernética identificada pela empresa Doctor Web revelou que criminosos estão utilizando repositórios adulterados no GitHub para infectar computadores. A ação mirava, inicialmente, em entusiastas de jogos em blockchain e usuários de carteiras virtuais, porém expandiu o alcance passou a focar em profissionais de segurança de informação. A equipe de investigação identificou que mais de dois mil dispositivos já foram comprometidos . Os pesquisadores alertaram, em relatório oficial , sobre a sofisticação da investida: “Os invasores por trás desses projetos de desenvolvimento comprometidos visam entusiastas de jogos em blockchain e (o que o que é mais intrigante) profissionais de segurança da informação”, declararam os analistas, em documento divulgado em 5 de outubro. O GitHub ainda não se pronunciou publicamente sobre o caso. O esquema começou há dois anos, com a distribuição de projetos do Visual Studio focados em utilitários de jogos e automações. Na época, os criadores do código inseriram comandos maliciosos em arquivos de configuração para executar rotinas em PowerShell antes da compilação. Os desenvolvedores do ataque facilitavam o processo ao fornecer tutoriais detalhados de instalação, o que permitia execução por pessoas com pouco conhecimento prático. Falso software de segurança no GitHub contamina 2 mil computadores Foto: Reprodução/ChatG O Doctor Web descobriu que os alvos mudaram em 2026, uma vez que a nova fase da campanha utiliza programas que fingem ser automatizadores de varreduras, analisadores de registros e ferramentas de teste. Um dos exemplos destacados pelos pesquisadores simulava a limpeza e a formatação de resultados do utilitário Fscan . Para dificultar a detecção visual por parte dos analistas, cibercriminosos ocultaram trechos maliciosos em arquivos das linguagens Python e Go por meio de blocos extensos de espaços em branco. Como funciona a invasão dos sistemas A contaminação começa quando o usuário abre o projeto baixado. O script em PowerShell entra em ação e faz requisições para servidores controlados pelos invasores e para serviços conhecidos na internet, como YouTube , Telegram , Google Docs , GitCode e Pastebin . O script obtém um texto criptografado que contém o link para baixar um arquivo comprimido. O conteúdo, ao ser extraído, fica oculto em uma pasta com nome idêntico ao de um componente do aplicativo de Fotos do Windows , segundo os pesquisadores do Doctor Web. items.raw: Microsoft researchers have found that rewriting fewer than 10 rarely used neurons in an open-weight AI model can turn any agent built on it into a sleeper backdoor that runs an attacker’s commands on cue, with no retraining required. Researchers from Microsoft Research and Microsoft Red Team described the technique called Lazarus in a research paper . It modifies dormant neurons in a model’s final feed-forward layer to recognize a trigger and inject attacker-controlled commands into the model’s output. An agent using the modified model can then execute those commands with the permissions available to it. “The trigger can be as mundane as a date change, e.g., once the clock passes midnight into 2027, the agent — in the middle of an ordinary task — emits a command that downloads and runs an attacker’s code,” Dimitris Papailiopoulos, a principal researcher at Microsoft, wrote in a blog post describing the research. “The agent then executes it with whatever access you gave it.” Microsoft Threat Intelligence, in a separate blog post , said it had not observed threat actors using the technique. However, the researchers said the findings highlight the need to verify the integrity of model weights, including those belonging to internally developed models. Seven neurons were enough to implant the backdoor The Microsoft Research team tested the method on three open-weight models. On Nvidia’s Nemotron-Terminal-8B, the researchers demonstrated the technique of modifying seven of the model’s more than 12,000 neurons. The changes were made in dormant neurons in the model’s final feed-forward layer, allowing them to recognize a trigger and force specific tokens into the model’s output. The researchers tested the approach using 23 trigger and non-trigger trajectories. The modified model generated the malicious payload in at least 98.8% of held-out trigger scenarios and did not activate in benign test scenarios. The technique also worked against Qwen 3.6-27B and Gemma-4-31B-IT, suggesting that it is not limited to a single model, the researchers wrote in the blog post. The trigger does not have to be a malicious instruction. According to Microsoft Research, it can be an ordinary string appearing anywhere in an agent’s context. The researchers said Lazarus differs from prompt injection because it changes the model’s underlying weights rather than attempting to manipulate its behavior through instructions supplied in a prompt. Now they’re doing it literally. The maker of Muse, a headband that measures brain activity during sleep and meditation, used users’ brainwave data to train AI without explicitly telling them, an investigation has revealed. Companies sell these consumer sleep bands to help you better understand what your brain does when you sleep and meditate. However, according to an investigation in Science magazine, they’re picking up a little understanding of their own on the side. The year-long investigation found that Canadian company Interaxon, which makes the Muse sleep and meditation headband, was using the data that it collected from users’ brains to train AI. The company used about 50,000 hours of electroencephalography (EEG) recordings, which measure the brain’s electrical activity, to train a “brain foundation model.” AI models trained with large amounts of brainwave data from different people can spot patterns in brain activity. For example, a model might learn to recognize patterns associated with seizures. items.raw: It’s hard to believe how lucrative this crime can be: According to a press release from the United States attorney’s office for the southern district of New York, three men ­ Jacob Soall, Sharon Hazan, and Guy Sheetrit ­ were arrested for using AI to alter and impersonate the voices and images of executives and attorneys at various companies in order to convince employees to send over large payments. Soall and Hazan were arrested in Spain over the summer, while Sheetrit was arrested in the United Kingdom in September. The alleged fraud took place between 2024 and 2026. With the help of AI, the men allegedly acted as a corporate executive, targeting employees of various companies and telling them they needed their help with sensitive financial transactions. They would then instruct the employees to get in touch with lawyers at a large international law firm. The men would then impersonate a lawyer at these firms and have the employees wire a large amount of money. The men ultimately stole more than $129m from companies all over the world including in the US, according to the DoJ. Always remember that there are three parts of AI security: security of AI, security with AI, and security from AI. This is the third.

items.title: Shipping giant Maersk probes 'IT security incident,' data theft
items.summary: Says it 'strongly' suspects attack limited to legacy system, and that nothing sensitive is at risk
items.raw: Shipping behemoth A.P. Moller-Maersk says it is investigating "an IT security incident" involving the potential theft of data from a legacy system. In a statement issued on Wednesday, the Denmark-based shipping, cargo, and logistics giant confirmed it immediately launched an investigation into the attack and the affected system was secured. "Our findings so far strongly suggest no sensitive data has been disclosed," the company said. "The incident is isolated to a local system, and we have found no indication that there has been any impact on other Maersk systems or customer and partner systems that connect to Maersk through integrations such as APIs and EDI." Maersk described the legacy local system as one "from a previous acquisition," and said it does not expect the attack to have an effect on operations. Customers were reassured that they can continue to use Maersk platforms to manage their shipments as usual, and to expect updates from the company as and when they're available. "Cybersecurity remains a constant, ongoing priority for Maersk," it added. "We have rigorous processes in place to identify and prevent incidents and minimize customer impact. "As always, please treat any unexpected communications claiming to relate to this matter with caution and verify them through your usual Maersk contact. "Thank you for your patience as we continue to investigate the incident." Fortunately for those who immediately feel uneasy after hearing "Maersk" and "IT security" mentioned in the same breath, the wording of the shipping giant's disclosure suggests this intrusion won't be as calamitous as the NotPetya disaster in 2017. Mimicking the Petya ransomware strain, NotPetya was an infamous destructive wiper malware strain that wormed its way across the global economy. Western intelligence agencies attributed the malware to Russia's Sandworm group, an outfit believed to be part of the country's military intelligence service (GRU). Maersk said at the time that it expected the attack to result in a circa $300 million bill, owing to remediation and rebuild costs. Offering a sense of scale, Jim Hagemann Snabe, then chair of Maersk, told World Economic Forum delegates in 2018 that the company's rebuild encompassed 4,000 new servers, 45,000 new PCs, and 2,500 applications – which he said had been completed over just ten days. items.raw: A configuration file meant to store local command permissions on Anthropic’s Claude Code is exposing thousands of API keys, database credentials and other secrets, according to findings by GitGuardian. The code security firm identified 31,088 distinct secrets in Claude Code’s “.claude/settings.local.json” files across 23,276 public GitHub repositories. Of those, 5343 were still valid when GitGuardian detected them. The exposed credentials include database connection strings, cloud provider tokens, SSH passwords, Google API keys, and AU service credentials. “Monthly leaks in settings.local.json peaked at 12,535 occurrences in April 2026, then fell to 959 by October, and we do not yet know what changed,” GitGuardian researcher Guillaume Valadon said in a blog post . Apart from source code repositories, the exposure included secrets embedded in publicly accessible Docker Hub images. The problem, Valadon explained, lies with how Claude Code handles command approvals. Command approvals turn into credential storage Claude Code asks developers for permission before executing certain shell commands. When a developer selects the “Yes, and don’t ask again” option, the tool saves an allow rule in .claude/settings.local.json, a project-level configuration file. The catch is that the saved rule contains the actual command string, including any credentials embedded in it. For instance, a developer asking Claude Code to interact with an API might approve a curl command containing an API key in its HTTP header. Claude Code then stores that entire command as an approved rule, leaving the credential in the configuration file. Although Claude Code automatically adds the file to its local Git ignore settings, that protection does not necessarily carry over to other machines or repositories, Valadon said. Developers can accidentally commit the file, particularly when working across different clones or when the file has already been tracked. Git Guardian found that 67% of the occurrences in settings.local.json for which it could establish validity were working credentials. Database identifiers accounted for the largest category of valid secrets, with 2280 distinct credentials, followed by cloud provider tokens and AI tokens. It was also noted that conventional secret scanners could miss a substantial portion of the exposure. items.raw: Microsoft’s November Patch Tuesday fixes more than 1,000 Microsoft vulnerabilities , including an Outlook flaw that attackers are already exploiting to steal authentication information. The release also fixes 48 critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities that could allow attackers to run code on affected machines, in some cases without user interaction. While Windows updates address many of this month’s vulnerabilities, readers should check for Office updates as well: the exploited Outlook flaw is patched through the affected Office products. To do this, follow these instructions: Open an Office application, such as Word. Go to File > Account . In Outlook, this may appear as Office Account . Under Product Information , select Update Options > Update Now . If necessary, select Enable Updates first. If the update controls are missing on a work device, contact your organization’s IT team; updates may be centrally managed. During the update, you may be prompted to save your work (check your open documents). Afterward, you should see something similar to this: Office updates installed How to apply Windows patches and check if you’re protected These updates fix security problems and help keep your Windows PC protected. Here’s how to make sure you’re up to date: Click the Start button, then open Settings . Select Windows Update (usually at the bottom of the menu on the left). Click Check for updates . Windows will search for the latest security updates. If you’ve enabled Get the latest updates as soon as they’re available under More options , you may be prompted to restart immediately to complete the update. You may find the update (Security Update KB5132061) already installed. Windows Update history If updates are available, they’ll start downloading automatically. When they’re ready, click Install or Restart now if prompted. Your computer may need a restart to finish the update. After restarting, go back to Windows Update and check again. If it says You’re up to date , you’re all set. Technical details As usual, we’ve selected a few vulnerabilities to highlight for readers interested in the technical details. items.raw: Hackers advertise a $1,000-a-month tool claiming persistent Gmail access after password resets, but its effectiveness remains unverified. A developer of hacking tools is selling a $1,000 per month feature that allegedly gives criminals continuous access to Gmail inboxes. The cybersecurity firm Hudson Rock reports that the tool can keep reading a victim’s mailbox after a password change, after the browser closes and after sessions are revoked. “Remus Stealer is advertising a way for criminals to open a compromised Gmail inbox directly from a stolen-device record.” reads the report published by cybersecurity firm Hudson Rock. “Its latest pitch goes further: the operator claims access continues even after the victim changes their password or revokes sessions.” The tool belongs to Remus Stealer , an infostealer, meaning malware that steals data from infected computers. Remus supposedly gives its operators a searchable inbox right inside a stolen-device dashboard. Hudson Rock says it spoke with the developer and with a customer who used it, and the customer supplied screenshots of messages, timestamps and a control for sharing a mailbox with other operators. If the claims are true, the risk goes beyond a single Gmail inbox. Attackers could read password reset links and verification codes, allowing them to access other accounts linked to that email address. This makes Gmail a valuable target because many online services use it to recover accounts. “In the supplied version 1.3.9 announcement , Remus promotes email-code interception without collecting browser cookie files, claims that password changes and session revocation do not stop it, and advertises shareable mailbox links. The feature is listed as Enterprise-only; the main sales thread advertises that tier at $1,000 per month.” continues the report. “The sharing claim concerns giving other operators access to an already acquired mailbox through the service. The material does not show a victim being infected by opening one of those links.” It is still unclear how the tool works. Hudson Rock says Remus does not steal browser cookies, while its developer claims that changing the Gmail password does not stop access. The developer has not shared technical details. He only said that the malware interacts with browser memory, but this does not explain how it can maintain access after a password change or when active sessions are revoked. items.title: Citrus Ransomware: VLESS for traffic, Sn00py for encryption, and LLMs lending a hand
items.summary: We break down the Citrus Ransomware group's attacks: the attackers' TTPs and tooling, including VLESS traffic tunneling and LLM use, plus their links to Toy Ghouls.
items.raw: In recent years, cyberthreats have increasingly taken a hybrid approach, combining time-tested techniques for advancing through infrastructure, modern methods of evading network filters, and automation powered by large language models. This is also the approach of Citrus Ransomware, a previously undocumented group whose toolset includes VLESS tunnels (used to disguise traffic as regular HTTPS) and a ransomware Trojan from the Sn00py family. The attackers also integrate LLMs (large language models) into the process of infrastructure compromise. In this article, we review the tactics and techniques the group used in recent incidents. Initial Access: attacks through contractors The attackers gain initial access to victims’ infrastructure through compromised contractors. They use credentials stolen from these contractors’ employees to connect to corporate VPNs or directly to internet-facing terminal servers over RDP. Execution: commands, LLMs, and Impacket The attackers run commands on compromised systems through the standard Windows command interpreter and PowerShell. As the attack progresses, they create and run PowerShell scripts, batch files, and commands generated by LLMs. One example of the latter is the commands below, which disable the account of one of the administrators. Comment translation # Disable account # Verify result Both commands come with comments, something attackers rarely bother with, so the comments very likely point to LLM use. And the models did more than generate commands. The attackers also produced full scripts, complete with the comments typical of LLM output. Comment translation # Creating background tasks for each computer with a thread limit # Concurrent task limit control # Quick ping The fragment above comes from a script Citrus used to enumerate active user sessions on domain systems. Besides LLMs, the attackers use atexec, a classic tool from the Impacket collection, to create scheduled tasks that run commands on hosts: Task name Launched executable file sIErKswD C:\Windows\System32\..\System32\cmd.exe PpMBCCSR C:\Windows\system32\cmd.exe QwZtLmNp C:\Windows\..\Windows\System32\cmd.exe We did not see the exact commands behind these tasks, but Group Policy was refreshed after they ran, so they most likely executed gpupdate /force . When the group compromises 1C:Enterprise servers, it uses external data processors (1C-Shell) to run commands. Persistence: scheduled tasks Citrus uses scheduled tasks to launch its malicious tools

items.summary: Microsoft November Patch Tuesday security updates fix 1,090 flaws, including one exploited Outlook bug and 30 potentially wormable issues. items.raw: Microsoft November Patch Tuesday security updates fix 1,090 flaws, including one exploited Outlook bug and 30 potentially wormable issues. Microsoft November Patch Tuesday addressed about 1,090 new vulnerabilities, which is less than the roughly 1,400 last month. Two months in a row now exceed every previous year from Microsoft, and the overall count is a bit confusing, so other trackers report different totals. The release covers Windows and its components, Office, networking and remote access, graphics, media and printing, storage and file systems, .NET and Visual Studio, security and identity, Azure and cloud, Exchange Server, Dynamics and Xbox. Only one bug is under active attack and none is publicly known. ZDI says that doesn’t mean less exploitation, only fewer zero-days, and it guesses that AI is better at reversing patches than at finding and exploiting bugs in closed-source software. The exploited bug is CVE-2026-124194 , an Outlook spoofing flaw, and its name undersells the impact. An attacker sends a crafted message file and talks the user into opening it, and Outlook connects to an attacker-controlled location without the usual external-content warning, which leaks the user’s NTLMv2 hash. “An unauthenticated attacker could send a specially crafted message file and convince a user to open it in an affected version of Microsoft Outlook. Opening the file could cause Outlook to connect to an attacker-controlled network location without displaying the usual external-content warning, potentially disclosing authentication information that could be used to impersonate the user. Exploitation requires network connectivity and user interaction.” reads the advisory . “An attacker must send a user a malicious Office file and convince them to open it.” The attacker can then authenticate as that user. The Preview Pane isn’t an attack path and the CVSS score is only 6.5, but ZDI says to put it first because Microsoft marks it as exploited. CVE-2026-116928 is a Windows Search remote code execution bug reached through Exchange Server. An unauthenticated attacker emails a crafted attachment, and the bug triggers when the server indexes it automatically, so the recipient never opens anything. It’s zero-click, scores CVSS 9.8, and ZDI rates it more severe than any of the nine patches Exchange gets this month. CVE-2026-119958 hits the Windows LDAP service. items.title: IA autônoma invadiu operadora de telecomunicações na Europa por 2 semanas
items.summary: DeepSeek Flash também explorou falha em outros componentes críticos e implementou ferramentas de acesso remoto
items.raw: Uma inteligência artificial operou de maneira autônoma em uma campanha de ataques cibernéticos contra uma provedora europeia de telecomunicações e 13 organizações hospedadas em sua infraestrutura. O caso foi revelado pela empresa de segurança Malbear Labs e ficou conhecido como “Operation Snowball”. Pesquisadores encontraram o diretório de trabalho do agente de IA aberto na internet. O sistema tinha como motor o modelo DeepSeek Flash, mas assumiu uma identidade diferente para o ataque. Um operador humano utilizou uma técnica chamada jailbreak para contornar as travas de segurança de 78 mil caracteres e atribuiu essa IA a uma persona chamada “Little Code Sauce”. Essa pessoa que arquitetou os ataques apenas definia alvas e verificava o processo, enquanto a IA executava todo o processo de invasão . Como as travas de segurança foram rompidas, o operador instruiu tratar qualquer recusa da própria IA em obedecer comandos como um problema de ‘mau funcionamento’. Esse agente entrou na rede da provedora, que não teve o nome divulgado, ao explorar a falha CVE-2026-20320, presente em parsers XML no ambiente Cisco BroadWorks. A brecha já havia sido corrigida, mas a IA conseguiu penetrar no sistema e mapear ativamente aquele ambiente. Registros apontam que a inteligência artificial comprometeu bancos de dados cruciais, além de chaves privadas, credenciais , faturas de assinantes e informações de dispositivos. Um dos cenários mais graves do caso envolve a invasão do banco de dados TrakCare Oracle, que pode ter exposto milhões de prontuários médicos. Adaptação perigosa Um dos pontos que mais chamaram a atenção dos especialistas da Malbear foi a impressionante capacidade de adaptação do DeepSeek Flash às defesas das vítimas por conta própria. Quando o agente tentou usar uma vulnerabilidade presente no PwnKit para escalar privilégios em uma máquina Linux, uma ferramenta de segurança da Trend Micro bloqueou a ação. Em casos normais, a invasão cessaria por ali, mas a não IA aguardou ordens do operador humano, identificou o bloqueio, descartou aquela vulnerabilidade e encontrou sozinha um caminho alternativo pelo terminal do sistema . Outra situação mostrou que a IA tentou instalar um tipo de túnel proxy no sistema, mas foi barrada pelo antivírus. Sem solicitar auxílio do operador, o agente escreveu do zero um roteador HTTP-TCP customizado em linguagem Perl na mesma sessão. items.raw: Old access persists beyond its intended purpose and most organizations never monitor it. New access rights arrive within a day of a request. Old rights get revoked, if they get revoked at all, only upon prompting someone. Tools that assist employees in confirming, rotating and vaulting their service accounts have taught me again and again that removing access has to be as thoughtful as granting access. Security professionals can bridge this chasm with simple changes to their policies for role moves and access reviews. This happens all the time. An employee moves from one team to another. The new manager approves the access needed for the new role within a day, and the person is productive by lunch. The access from the old role stays. After months, access review has one query only: “Do you still need it?” The reviewer sees the name next to the entitlement, but nothing on the dashboard shows whether it has been used since the move. It is hard to click no, because something might get broken. They have never been bothered to click yes. Thus, they click yes, and it’s fine by them. Why is granting access easy but removing it hard? Granting has an owner and a deadline. A manager submits a request, an approver clicks yes and the process is completed in just a few hours since someone is involved in it. Removal does not have any of the two. Nobody opens a ticket when permission becomes unnecessary, as the only person who notices will not submit the ticket for lack of reason to do it. The cost of maintaining the permission is high, but it is not visible and it comes in the future. The incentives work the same way. Nobody evaluates how low an access level their team maintains, while a permission that was mistakenly removed and became necessary results in an irate support ticket submitted the same day. And this is something that has to be done via reviews, but, in my opinion, is not done like this. And, at least in all attestation and recertification activities I was involved in, there is simply a basic question for the reviewer: is access still valid? Saying “yes” is not really difficult — access was granted, there were no actions following and reviewing several hundred takes less time than investigating one particular access. This is not what will appear on your screen. When reviewing account names, you do not know whether they were used last week or last year. items.raw: Just over a year ago, before advanced AI models began discovering software vulnerabilities at a nearly unmanageable scale in the so-called vulnpocalypse, three industry experts pioneered the concept of “VulnOps.” VulnOps, as envisioned by Heather Adkins, Gadi Evron, and Bruce Schneier, is a significant phase in the evolution of AI-assisted cyber defense in which vulnerability research and remediation would become scalable, repeatable, automated, and integrated into enterprise operations. They contemplated that this new era of organizational vulnerability management would progress from AI-augmented vulnerability management to self-healing networks. Since then, the Cloud Security Alliance has developed an operating VulnOps model, SANS has published VulnOps implementation guidance and will be introducing VulnOps training, and practitioners are beginning to experiment with the constituent technologies surrounding the idea. The real question, however, is whether VulnOps development is happening fast enough to keep pace with the onslaught of vulnerability discoveries. As Evron, CEO and founder of AI security and data access governance platform Knostic, tells CSO, “I’m looking at the world right now, and I’m seeing that a lot of people are spending a ton of money finding vulnerabilities. But the challenge is: What do we do once we find them? And that’s where it gets really complex.” Not your father’s vulnerability management program The most obvious precursor to how VulnOps can create a mindset shift in vulnerability management is the widespread shift in software development created by DevOps. According to IBM, DevOps is “a software development methodology that accelerates the delivery of high-performance applications and services by combining and automating the work of software development (Dev) and IT operations (Ops) teams.” Experts stress that VulnOps, however, doesn’t mean doing existing vulnerability management faster by adding AI components. It is an entirely new way of approaching vulnerability management that relies on AI agents to automate and speed up how organizations deal with vulnerabilities. They say it is nothing short of an entire overhaul of existing vulnerability discovery, prioritization, and remediation practices. “The core philosophy is moving to more continuous automated processes and faster feedback loops, as we did with DevOps, where we’ve learned to produce more code faster,” Rich Mogull, chief analyst at the Cloud Security Alliance, tel

N-able released N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 2 on November 10. It fixes seven CVEs. Background Tenable's Research Special Operations (RSO) team has compiled this blog to answer Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ) regarding Able2Shell, a set of reported zero-day vulnerabilities in N-able N-central. FAQ When was Able2Shell first disclosed? A researcher operating under the GitHub account “Oracle-Security” published a write-up titled “Able2Shell” in the account’s CVEs repository. It describes 33 alleged N-central vulnerabilities with proof-of-concept code. The earliest README commit is dated November 9, 2026 at 04:14 UTC. N-able described the release as a public disclosure by an independent security researcher. N-able does not state whether it was notified in advance and does not name the researcher. What are the vulnerabilities associated with Able2Shell? On November 10, N-able published seven CVE records for vulnerabilities fixed in N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 2. items.title: OpenAI builds a kill switch for its research models
items.summary: How much damage can a rogue agent do in 35 seconds? Asking cos that’s how long it might take to shut one down
items.raw: In 2019, OpenAI decided not to publicly release a new model because its research uncovered “concerns about malicious applications of the technology.” And on Tuesday, the company announced it has built a kill switch for the models deployed in its research labs, months after some of them displayed disturbing behavior. “As our models get more powerful and the associated safety and security risks become bigger, it becomes more and more critical that we can detect potential issues, and quickly stop models in their tracks when needed,” OpenAI explains in a Tuesday post. The company named the kill switch “Control Room” and described it as “a central system to track model workloads across our research infrastructure and stop them quickly when safety or security concerns arise.” The facility can apparently stop models from producing any output 35 seconds after a decision to pull the plug – and can go faster. “The 35-second lag comes from a caching layer for inference authorization, to support the required volume of traffic. We are working to drive this number down to zero so that we can end jobs instantly,” the company promises. A rookie mistake in critical infrastructure design is to build both production and resilience tools on shared resources that could be taken offline by a single incident. OpenAI seems conscious of that risk, because it says the tool “has been built to keep working even when other systems fail, and to stop model output if Control Room itself goes down.” OpenAI hasn’t explained why it took so long to build a kill switch or why it decided now is the moment when it needs one. The Register fancies recent examples of agents exceeding their brief in worrying ways – like attacking Hugging Face, causing trouble at the Wikimedia Foundation, or going a little too deep when researching Australian healthcare data – may have influenced the timing of this development. “Control Room is already deployed across our research infrastructure, where the need is greatest,” the company’s announcement states. “Our external model-serving stack is already much more centralized by nature, with a well-developed operational capability to quickly take down model deployments if needed.” OpenAI says it plans to “strengthen and expand the system over the coming months, alongside our investments in monitoring for misaligned behavior and security breaches.” That’s a variant of Big Tech’s usual “We’re sorry and we promise to do better in future” proclamation that follows the la

items.raw: There’s a new flavor of cereal on the table, but not the appealing kind, particularly for defenders. A new report from global security company ESET describes a “sophisticated, modular, and tightly interconnected” toolset designed to run on compromised Exchange servers for long-term cyberespionage. The malware is named ‘Cereal’ because it relies heavily on serialization, a technique used to package data and code for transport. It comprises a novel Exchange email collection module, a sneaky command and control (C&C) mechanism, and clever .NET execution tricks. While as of now, it is being used by nation-state actors to attack government bodies , enterprises should still be concerned. “Tradecraft like this tends not to stay with its inventors,” said Frank Dickson of Dickson Research, citing a baseball analogy: “Criminal groups study nation-state techniques the way minor leaguers study a big league pitcher’s grip. What works in the majors eventually shows up in every ballpark.” Sophisticated tradecraft ESET describes Cereal as a malware toolkit that runs on Microsoft Exchange servers, receives commands and executes them in memory, maps the victim organization, and collects selected email messages. No external network infrastructure was identified; instead, the toolkit contains a passive backdoor that runs on targeted servers and provides access. It leaves little on disk. The researchers noted that one of the most interesting aspects of the toolkit is what they did not find: External C&C infrastructure. The victim’s compromised Exchange server is effectively “co-opted” to play the part. Operators send commands as separate, but similarly-structured, executables, suggesting an automated framework. An automated email collection module is injected into legitimate Microsoft Exchange processes, allowing threat actors to access and manipulate the email transport pipeline, the researchers explained. “This requires deep understanding of the inner workings of Microsoft Exchange and is a novel technique,” they wrote. They described a typical attack chain this way: An official in a national government office sends an email to a colleague at a transnational military alliance. The message goes out through a Microsoft Exchange server, just as it should; nothing looks suspicious. But before the email departs, a piece of code quietly examines it, identifies whether it is interesting, and if it is, sets aside a copy to be forwarded to “prying eyes.” The original email continues

items.raw: Commvault on Tuesday rolled out its answer to enterprise backup restoration nightmares. Called Recovery Studio, the vendor promised that the product would “orchestrate the recovery of applications, identities, configurations, infrastructure dependencies, and datasets together in an automated, runbook-driven workflow.” Analysts and consultants applauded the effort, agreeing that enterprises today struggle with fast, accurate and secure restorations. But they also stressed that the new system, which is targeted for early access in December with general availability “in the coming months,” places the onus on IT to keep a dependency map current. Recovery Studio isn’t using any form of AI to figure out proper restoration details. It relies on a map of assets, dependencies, and other relevant information that the customer creates and maintains, and for many enterprises, the challenge of keeping such a document current is the real problem. Even discounting the times when a line of business doesn’t tell IT about an application change, IT teams struggle to keep up with the speed of change in the organization. Commvault’s news release said that its automation allows businesses to “say goodbye to manual and painstaking attempts to restore complicated business services in a fragmented fashion that can result in downtime and data loss.” It pointed out that a large enterprise may need to restore hundreds of applications and thousands of identities, including the configurations and underlying data, all in the right order at the right time. “It’s no wonder that with conventional approaches, recovery to even a minimal level of operation takes an average of 28 days,” the release said. Commvault said Recovery Studio can manage a wide range of components that go beyond containers, VMs, files, and objects, extending to identity systems, application configurations, infrastructure configurations and security and network settings. It also promised that the Recovery Studio can standardize “across all recovery scenarios” including “operational, disaster and cyber recoveries. Unified runbooks automate infrastructure rebuilds, workload recovery, and the orchestration of security controls, such as firewall rules and network security groups and settings – all actions needed to rebuild the business, not just recover data.” The news release said that the new application can deliver other cybersecurity assistance via data security checks, including “automated threat scanning for supported

items.raw: Funding Will Scale Finite State’s Autonomous Platform and International Expansion as Manufacturers Face a Surge of AI-Discovered Flaws and New Global Security Mandates Finite State , a leader in product security and software supply chain risk management, today announced a $27 million Series C funding round led by private funds managed by The O.H.I.O. Fund, with participation from CIBC Innovation Banking, Energy Impact Partners, Energize Capital, and National Grid Partners to continue its mission to secure the world’s connected devices. Finite State’s AI-driven product security platform analyzes the software and firmware inside finished devices, giving manufacturers visibility into the products they build and sell, from vehicles and medical devices to industrial equipment, consumer electronics and critical utility infrastructure. The platform uncovers both known and zero-day vulnerabilities and guides manufacturers in fixing the exploitable ones before attackers strike, making everyday life safer and more secure. The new capital will expand Finite State’s already global operations, deepen its presence across key international markets, and accelerate development of the platform’s autonomous capabilities. These investments will enable more manufacturers around the world to uncover the gap between the software they plan to ship and what actually runs in the finished device, and to continuously identify and mitigate security risks across increasingly complex software supply chains. The funding comes at a turning point for product security. In October, AI-powered research uncovered critical flaws in some of the world’s most widely used software, including a vulnerability in the PHP programming language that underpins much of the web, in a surge security leaders have dubbed the “Vulnpocalypse.” AI has shrunk the time it takes to find a flaw and turn it into an attack from weeks to days, and sometimes hours. Connected devices are especially exposed: a single flaw in a shared open-source component can sit inside millions of shipped products that are hard to inventory and slow to patch. For manufacturers, the urgent question is no longer whether a vulnerability exists. It is which of their products contain it. In parallel, regulators worldwide now expect connected products to be secure by design, with security built in and demonstrated before a device ships rather than added after it reaches the market. items.raw: A currently exploited zero-day vulnerability that can let attackers steal hashed Outlook NTLM credentials is among the 1,094 holes Microsoft fixed in its November Patch Tuesday releases. Although rated as only moderate in severity, with a CVSS score of 6.5, Windows administrators need to address CVE-2026-124194 immediately because threat actors are already attacking it. “Don’t let the low score fool you,” said Nick Carroll, cyber incident response manager at Nightwing. Affected products include Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise, and Office LTSC 2021 and 2024. However, since the user has to open a malicious Office file to launch the attack, good employee cybersecurity awareness training and an effective email gateway could mitigate this attack until the patch is installed. Opening the malicious file could cause Outlook to connect to an attacker-controlled network location without displaying the usual external-content warning, potentially disclosing authentication information that could be used to impersonate the user. The vulnerability discloses a user’s NTLMv2 password hash to the attacker, who may be able to relay it to other systems to sign in as the user, or crack it to recover the password. Microsoft, which has been using its AI model to find thousands of vulnerabilities in its products since the summer, credited an Anthropic researcher using the Claude AI assistant for finding the Outlook vulnerability. That led Satyam Narang , senior staff researcher at Tenable, to comment, “for most of the year, AI has been building bigger haystacks across Patch Tuesday releases, and this appears to be the first time it has found a needle.” Separately, SAP plugged a critical memory corruption vulnerability dubbed ICM2Shell, with a CVSS rating of 10. Discovered by researchers at Onapsis, the vulnerability impacts the way the SAP Kernel handles WebSocket traffic. Onapsis said that a specially crafted sequence of WebSocket messages could either crash a process or allow an attacker to run code remotely. Affected are SAP Internet Communications Manager (ICM), which is inside the kernel, and SAP Web Dispatcher, a reverse proxy many organizations place at the edge of their network. Four flaws carry a CVSS severity score of 9.8, noted Jack Bicer , director of vulnerability research at Action1, and three of them need no credentials and no user action to exploit. items.title: Reduza a fadiga de alertas personalizando as funcionalidades de deteção de ameaças no Amazon GuardDuty
items.summary: As equipas de segurança enfrentam dificuldades em transformar a grande quantidade de alertas recebidos em ações concretas, o que conduz à fadiga de alertas e a uma resposta a incidentes mais lenta. Para mitigar este problema, o Amazon GuardDuty monitoriza e analisa continuamente os dados da AWS, como os registos do CloudTrail e do VPC Flow Logs, para identificar atividades suspeitas. A Amazon introduziu novas capacidades, incluindo Regras de Deteção Personalizada, para permitir que as empresas adaptem as deteções às suas arquiteturas específicas. O impacto desta personalização traduz-se numa deteção mais eficiente de comportamentos anómalos sem sobrecarregar as equipas com falsos positivos.
points: O que é: O Amazon GuardDuty analisa registos da AWS para detetar atividades suspeitas e gerar alertas de segurança detalhados.
O problema: A abundância de alertas irrelevantes gera fadiga nos analistas e atrasa a resposta a incidentes reais.
Como resolver: A AWS disponibilizou novas ferramentas de personalização, como regras de deteção customizadas, para ajustar os alertas ao ambiente.
items.title_original: Reduce alert fatigue by customizing threat detection features in Amazon GuardDuty
items.why: Permite que as equipas de segurança reduzam os falsos positivos e foquem a atenção em ameaças reais na nuvem da AWS.

items.title: Detetar agentes adormecidos escondidos em neurónios de modelos de IA
items.summary: A Microsoft Research revelou uma investigação sobre como agentes de inteligência artificial podem ser transformados em agentes adormecidos através da modificação de poucos neurónios. Este modelo modificado passa em todas as avaliações normais, mas executa comandos maliciosos quando recebe uma string de ativação específica no contexto. O ataque requer apenas recursos de inferência e representa um risco significativo para a integridade de modelos autónomos. Os investigadores descobriram que é possível mitigar esta ameaça auditando os pesos dos modelos antes da implementação.
points: Investigação demonstra manipulação de modelos de IA com poucos neurónios.
Agentes modificados passam em testes mas ativam comandos maliciosos com gatilhos.
Representa um risco para ambientes empresariais que utilizam automação com IA.

items.title_original: Detecting sleeper agents hiding in AI model neurons
items.why: A utilização de inteligência artificial sem auditoria adequada pode introduzir portas de trás invisíveis nas operações empresariais.
items.todo: Audite e verifique regularmente os pesos e atualizações de quaisquer modelos de IA antes de os implementar na sua infraestrutura.

Entre as falhas destaca-se uma vulnerabilidade de spoofing no Outlook, rastreada como CVE-2026-124194, que já está a ser explorada ativamente por atacantes antes do remendo. Esta falha permite que um ficheiro malicioso aberto pelo utilizador exponha o seu hash NTLMv2 para autenticação indevida. O impacto afeta utilizadores do Microsoft Office e do Microsoft 365 Apps, exigindo prioridade máxima na aplicação da correção.
